summary:
Daejeon stands under South Korea's national legal framework, in which gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is lawful. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted, most visibly in the 2017 military operation that Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, under which 32 personnel were criminally charged and one gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Daejeon is where the sharpest documented harm to a trans person in South Korean military service was litigated. Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel treated the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. On 7 October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's discharge in what is recorded as the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier, holding that the military should have recognised her as female following her legal sex change, that loss of genitalia was not valid grounds for dismissal, and that fitness review should weigh basic rights. The decision vindicated her posthumous appeal. In March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Byun Hee-soo was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024, an official honour that did not settle the institutional question. About 60 activists attended and protested, arguing that the burial was marred by discriminatory treatment, and her case continues to be recorded against gender dysphoria classified as a mental disorder and a post-surgery physical-disability finding. Her state burial in Daejeon therefore coexists with an institutional stance that remains conservative.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korean courts and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled that mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years, and finding that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that had uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register; an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a live problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal available, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, and ordered symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state machinery. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
Daejeon's role in this record runs against the national grain in one respect and with it in another. The Daejeon District Court delivered the pro-recognition ruling that reversed a trans soldier's discharge, while the same city hosts the state cemetery where the military's treatment of her was formally contested by protesters at the burial. A visitor should not read the court ruling as evidence that the armed forces themselves have softened: article 92-6 stands, the Constitutional Court affirmed it in 2023, and transgender people remain outside military service by exclusion rather than by choice.

The trajectory of the Byun Hee-soo case is a reasonable proxy for how recognition advances in South Korea. It moved through discharge, death, posthumous judicial reversal, line-of-duty recognition by the Defence Ministry in March 2024, and burial with state honours in June 2024, with each step contested by activists who judged the treatment discriminatory. Recognition arrives case by case rather than through a general statute, which is also how gender recognition itself has moved: two Supreme Court and high-court rulings in 2022 and 2024 removed, respectively, the bar on trans parents and the surgical precondition.

Comparatively, the pattern in South Korea is protective machinery without a protective statute. There is a functioning National Human Rights Commission, active LGBTI organisations, a registry route for NGOs, and a Constitutional Court willing to grant partner healthcare rights, yet no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and repeated bureaucratic obstruction of registration litigation. Violence risk is concentrated and episodic: Pride events draw large counter-protests requiring thousands of police, and public-health contact tracing has previously produced outing on a mass scale.
localsOnly:

The 24 November 2022 Supreme Court decision separately removed the blanket bar on recognition for transgender people who have minor children, subject to not being married at the time.

Cisgender and post-operative residents of Daejeon who are called up face the exclusion rule: transgender people are barred from military service. Personnel already serving remain exposed to article 92-6 and to fitness-review practice of the kind applied to Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo, whose discharge the Daejeon District Court cancelled on 7 October 2021 on the grounds that loss of genitalia was not valid grounds for dismissal.

In everyday life, Daejeon residents share the national absence of any comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and no local instrument is recorded in the sources as filling that gap. Restroom use in public and educational settings remains contested: courts have awarded compensation against the state for advice that restricted a trans person's restroom access, and school-based research documents trans students withholding urine and leaving school early to avoid exposure.

Transgender residents seeking hospital care in Daejeon encounter the gap identified by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients. The state burial of Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024 is a matter of local record; about 60 activists protested that the burial was marred by discriminatory treatment.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 7 October 2021 Daejeon District Court decision was reviewed on further appeal, and its finality, is not stated in the available source and remains unresolved here; the source describes the ruling as vindicating a posthumous appeal without recording the procedural endpoint.

The outcome of the protest at Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo's burial on 24 June 2024, including whether the challenged discriminatory treatment was remedied or any complaint followed, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

No Daejeon-specific enforcement data, police conduct record, or local ordinance on gender identity or sexual orientation appears in the inventory. Local conditions in Daejeon on violence, hate crime, and service access are therefore inferred from the national picture and are not separately verified for this city.

The sources do not state whether Daejeon hosts a Pride event, an LGBTI organisation, or a trans-specific healthcare provider, nor whether any conversion-practice restriction applies locally. These remain not sourced.

It is unresolved from the inventory whether the March 2024 Defence Ministry line-of-duty recognition carried any compensation or reinstatement consequence beyond the formal designation.
